summary: This informational document describes aspects of the prep tool expected to be created when the xml2rfc version 3 specification is deployed. The tool prepares an author's XML into a canonical form for further processing.

plainLanguage.summary: Authors send in their document and a helper program tidies it up before final publishing. This describes what that tidying program does.

subtitle: What the xml2rfc v3 prep tool does to an author's XML before it becomes an Internet-Draft or an RFC.

tldr.problem: RFCs are moving from plain text to XML as the canonical format, but readers will use HTML, PDF, text and other outputs. Those outputs should come out the same, and today the XML lacks much of the data they need.
tldr.mechanism: A 'prep tool' runs over the author's XML and cleans it, fills in defaults, normalizes it, generates boilerplate and numbering, inlines external files and finalizes the result. Formatters then only need a straightforward syntactic translation.
tldr.outcome: The prepped XML becomes a permanent record from which any current or future output format can be rendered. The RFC says the details are expected to change with implementation experience.

facts.label: Modes
facts.value: I-D mode and RFC production mode

today: RFC 7998 is an Informational document from the IAB and has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes the prep tool in terms of the xml2rfc v3 vocabulary of RFC 7991 and says its details are expected to change.

sections.title: Why a Prep Tool Is Needed
sections.content:
As described in RFC 6949, the canonical format of the RFC Series has been plain text and is now changing to XML, using the xml2rfc v3 vocabulary from RFC 7991. Most people will still read RFCs as HTML, PDF or text.

To keep those outputs as uniform as possible, the translation from XML should be a straightforward syntactic translation. That needs data in the XML that is not there today. A program called the prep tool adds it, often as part of the xml2rfc process.

The RFC warns that its details are expected to change as the new toolsets are implemented, and that other implementers must not expect later changes to stay backwards-compatible.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer program fills in all the missing details of a document so that every kind of copy comes out looking the same.

sections.title: Usage Scenarios
sections.content:
The tool has two settings: Internet-Draft preparation ("I-D mode") and canonical RFC preparation ("RFC production mode"). Only a few things differ between them, such as the boilerplate and the date on the front page.

When the draft submission tool accepts v3 XML, it runs the file through the prep tool. If there are no errors it keeps two files: the submitted file and the prepped file. The prepped file records what the submitter attested to, including what any external references resolved to at that time, and the formatters use it to produce HTML, PDF and text.

During editing, the RFC Production Center runs the tool in RFC production mode and shows authors the results during AUTH48. After AUTH48 it runs the tool one last time, locks down the canonical XML and publishes all formats. The prepped XML can later be re-rendered or used for new formats.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper keeps both your original and the tidied copy, like keeping the rough draft and the neat copy of a school essay.

sections.title: The Processing Steps
sections.content:
Section 5 lists the steps in order. Wherever the tool would add an attribute or element that already exists, it checks the value, and if it is wrong it warns with the old and new values and replaces it. The steps fall into groups:

  • XML sanitization: process x:include elements, fully process and then remove any DTD, remove processing instructions, check validity against the RELAX NG schema in RFC 7991, and give an error if an anchor begins with s-, f-, t- or i-.
  • Defaults: insert version (value 3), seriesInfo, date, prepTime, list start values and other attribute defaults, and set each section's toc attribute to include or exclude.
  • Normalization: turn month values into numbers, drop redundant ascii attributes, and convert deprecated title attributes into name elements.
  • Generation: add expiresDate in I-D mode, create the boilerplate (Status of this Memo and Copyright Notice), add reference targets, slugified names, sorted references, pn part numbers, iref numbers and derived content for cross-references.
sections.plainLanguage: The tool goes down a checklist: clean up, fill blanks, make things consistent, then add the numbering and standard paragraphs.

sections.title: Inclusion, Cleanup and Finalization
sections.content:
The inclusion steps pull external files into the document. For artwork and sourcecode elements with a src attribute, the tool turns scheme-less sources into file: URIs relative to the file being processed, and gives an error if a file would come from outside that directory or its subdirectories or if the source has shell metacharacters. It then moves the data into the element's content and records the originalSrc.

RFC production mode adds cleanup: it removes note and section elements marked removeInRFC, removes cref elements and XML comments, removes xml:base and originalSrc attributes, and ensures the result fully complies with the v3 schema with no deprecated elements. It also checks link elements for the ISSN 2070-1721, a DOI and the source Internet-Draft.

Finalization fills in the scripts attribute from the characters used and pretty-formats the XML.
sections.plainLanguage: It pastes in any pictures or code the author pointed to, throws away the sticky notes, and makes the final page neat.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The inclusion rules are meant to stop artwork and sourcecode from exposing files outside the directory of the document being processed. For example, values starting with /, ./ or ../ should generate errors.

The security considerations in RFC 3470 also apply: processing XML external references can expose an implementation to threats by making it access external resources automatically, so arbitrary access to such references in data from untrusted sources should be disallowed.
sections.plainLanguage: The tool must not be tricked into reading private files from other places on the computer.
